Biomagnetic Imaging Lab · Progress update

BrainOmni on Source-Space Parcellated MEG

Reconstructing sensor geometry from atlas centroids lets a pretrained MEG foundation model read parcellated source data it was never designed to accept — and it performs better there than on real sensor recordings.

8 September 2026 Fae Negoro Advisor · Srikantan Nagarajan Cohorts · 161 parcel + 148 OSF

This update covers the parcellated dataset from Pooja. The question was whether BrainOmni can use source-space data that has no sensor layout, and whether adding it to the existing OSF cohort improves classification. The answer to the first is yes, clearly. The answer to the second is no, for a reason worth understanding.

Method

Fabricating geometry from atlas centroids

BrainOmni needs a (C, 6) array — a 3D position and orientation for every channel. Real MEG supplies this from the physical sensor array. Pooja's data has already been projected into 246 Brainnetome regions, so no sensor layout exists.

Following your suggestion, we built one from the atlas itself:

position
the region's centroid — the mean coordinate of every voxel assigned to it
orientation
the normalised origin→centroid vector, approximating the outward cortical surface normal at that region
normalisation
centred on the mean and scaled to unit RMS radius, matching exactly what preprocessing.py does to real sensor coordinates
regions
210 cortical only; the 36 subcortical regions were excluded for poor MEG sensitivity

Signals were then processed identically to the sensor pipeline: resampled 600 → 256 Hz, z-normalised per region, split into two 30-second segments. A single-subject check confirmed the tokeniser produces output of exactly the same shape as sensor data — (16, 160, 256) — with values in the same range (−3.30 to 3.79, versus −3.30 to 3.78 for OSF).

FINDING 1

Parcellated data outperforms real sensor data

Frozen BrainOmni-tiny features with logistic regression, 5-fold cross-validation, seed 123.

CohortNAccuracyAUCChance
Parcel — source level161 0.850 ± 0.051 0.922 ± 0.0470.522
OSF — sensor level148 0.831 ± 0.102 0.859 ± 0.0920.527
Both pooled309 0.832 ± 0.043 0.898 ± 0.0510.502

The parcel result exceeds sensor level on both metrics, with half the variance. Two caveats belong with this number: the cohorts are different people, so this is not a like-for-like comparison, and parcel-alone has only been run on BrainOmni-tiny — the base model was never evaluated on it.

FINDING 2

Pooling the cohorts costs accuracy

Combining both datasets gives 309 subjects but performs worse than the 161-subject parcel cohort alone. The diagnostic explains why.

Per-cohort standardisation — z-scoring each dataset against its own mean and scale — recovers part of the loss but does not close it:

ConfigurationAccuracyAUC
Parcel alone (161)0.8500.922
Pooled, cohort-centred0.8310.909
Pooled, raw0.8320.898

Implication

The domain shift is larger than the disease signal. Naive pooling of sensor-level and source-level representations is not a route to more training data, even after correcting for the mean offset. Any future combination would need domain adaptation rather than concatenation.

FINDING 3

Fine-tuning changes nothing, at any size or depth

Fourteen configurations on the pooled cohort: two model sizes, three unfreezing depths, two classifier heads, plus the frozen reference. Differential learning rates (backbone 1e-5, head 1e-4), warmup-cosine schedule, epoch chosen on an inner validation split never used for testing.

Configurationtiny — accbase — acctiny — AUCbase — AUC

Last-1 + LR0.8380.8380.9020.902

Last-2 + LR0.8480.8280.8900.895

Last-3 + LR0.8450.8280.8850.893

Paired bootstrap against frozen features, on identical resamples, confirms this. Every interval contains zero — including the AUC difference for last-1 + NN, which is −0.000.

The training curves show the mechanism directly.

Context

Where this leaves BrainOmni

On the OSF cohort — the only one where both exist — six handcrafted spectral features from the original eLife study outperform every BrainOmni configuration tested:

MethodCohortAccuracyAUC
Handcrafted spectral (AEC + band power)OSF, 1480.8720.925
BrainOmni frozen, bestOSF, 1480.8310.878
BrainOmni fine-tuned, bestOSF, 1480.7970.851

Scope of that claim. This is one model on one task with 148 subjects, and the handcrafted baseline is unusually strong — those features were selected by the original authors because they separate Alzheimer's in this cohort. The defensible statement is that a frozen BrainOmni representation does not outperform task-specific spectral features here, and fine-tuning does not close the gap at either model size or any depth. No handcrafted baseline exists yet for the parcel cohort, so the strongest BrainOmni result (0.850 / 0.922) has never been compared against one.

A separate observation from the PCA sweep

Sweeping ten classifiers across 1–50 principal components on the parcel features, every peak falls between 5 and 27 components — the discriminative signal occupies a very low-dimensional subspace of the 4096-dimensional representation. ExtraTrees reaches 0.894 at 14 components, above the logistic-regression headline of 0.850. That figure comes from 500 swept configurations and carries no honest confidence interval, so it characterises the feature space rather than standing as a result — but it does suggest the class boundary is not perfectly linear.

Open

Questions I need your input on

  • Was sign flipping applied to the parcellation? PCA-based parcellation leaves each region's sign arbitrary. If it was not corrected across subjects, regions contradict each other and every number here is a floor rather than a ceiling. This is a silent failure mode — nothing in the results would reveal it.
  • Do the two cohorts share subjects? 77 AD in the parcel data versus 78 in OSF is close enough to suspect overlap. If they overlap, the pooled results have leakage and need grouped cross-validation. The code supports this via SUBJECT_GROUPS, but it needs an ID mapping.
  • Cortical only, or include subcortical? We used 210 of 246 regions, excluding subcortical for poor MEG sensitivity. Worth confirming that is the right call for this atlas.
  • Given that pooling underperforms, is the combined fine-tune still the experiment you want? Fine-tuning on parcel data alone would test the same question on the stronger representation, at roughly half the compute.

Reproducibility

Methods

preprocessing
600 → 256 Hz via polyphase resampling (32/75), per-channel z-normalisation, two 30-second segments per subject. No band-pass or notch filtering.
frozen features
proj_out → blocks[:-1] → L2 normalise → mean over time windows → average the two segments. 4096-dim for tiny, 8192 for base.
cross-validation
Stratified 5-fold, shuffled, seed 123. Inner 15% validation split carved from the training fold for epoch selection; the test fold is logged but never used for any selection decision.
fine-tuning
AdamW, weight decay 0.05, betas (0.9, 0.99), eps 1e-6. Backbone 1e-5, head 1e-4. Warmup-cosine over 10% of steps, label smoothing 0.1, gradient clipping 1.0. 400 epochs for last-1, 200 for last-2 and last-3.
uncertainty
2000-resample bootstrap. Method comparisons are paired — both methods are evaluated on the same resample each iteration — and all metrics are computed on pooled out-of-fold predictions.
checkpointing
State persisted after every completed fold with per-fold seeding, so an interrupted run resumes and reproduces an uninterrupted one exactly.
